about: Fordwic (Fordwich), the king's toll landing for Canterbury at the tide's end on the Stour, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/fordwic.md and the spine (cast.aethelheard, whose home this is; cast.alcuin, cast.wighelm, cast.gervold, cast.sigewine, cast.thorkell, cast.cnut; threads riddle_road, book_road, silver_road, black_stones, price_of_england). A draft for the user to overwrite. Read the note first. Woven with the other ports of the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways with Sarre, Dofras, Lundenwic, Hamwic, Gipeswic and Dommoc (the port-reeve Bruman is now tied to a port-reeve of his own day in London), beats added in those ports, and the region's cards (Data/encounters/england_south_east_793.json) hung on the sites and the beats.
note: Fordwic itself is known in these years from two toll charters (Sawyer 29, 1612), a reeve's gift (S 1654), one writ (S 1092), one Domesday entry and a few coins and sherds. What a merchant comes for, the archbishop, the mint, the books and the market, is in Canterbury, two miles up the track, and the game's tables hang the city on this port; so four of the sites here are in or by the city and say so. Nobody of Fordwic is named before Bruman the port-reeve. Where the landing and the toll place of 793 lay is not known, no toll rate is known, and no church can be shown at Fordwic before the late eleventh century: Mass is heard in the city. The mint is Canterbury's; none is known at Fordwic. We do not say that Northmen ever rowed up the Stour: in 851 the ships came into the Thames mouth, in 1009 the army landed at Sandwich. Every invented person and site says so in its source.

ports.summary: Fordwic is a row of fenced plots on the low south bank of the Stour, at the last place the tide reaches, where the king's toll men take toll by the ship. It is the landing for Canterbury: the archbishop, his scribes, the moneyers and the abbey of the kings' graves are two miles up the track, behind a Roman wall. A merchant comes to sell to the two churches, to change silver into the king's new pennies, to buy a leaf of riddles or carry a book, and to hear what the archbishop's household knows before the rest of Kent does.
ports.seasons: Ships come up on the flood from Easter to Martinmas and go down on the ebb; in a dry summer the last reach is shallow and a laden boat waits for a spring tide. Hay is cut on the marsh after midsummer and the mares are driven off it before the winter floods. The city fills for the feasts of its saints, Augustine in the last week of May and, in later ages, Dunstan a week before him and Ælfheah after Easter.

history.text: A marsh 'called Stodmerch beside Fordeuuicum' is granted away: the first time the place is named.
history.source: Sawyer 7, a doubted text resting on a seventh-century record (dossier 1)

history.text: King Hlothhere grants land at Sturry, over the ford. It is the oldest English charter that survives as it was first written.

King Wihtred's law punishes gifts to idols, meat in a fast and a slave's work on Sunday. A stranger who leaves the track and does not blow his horn may be killed or taken. It is dated the sixth day of Rugern, the rye harvest.
Archbishop Tatwine dies, leaving forty riddles in Latin verse. A man called Eusebius adds sixty to make the hundred.
history.source: dossier 7 (Tatwine; Anglo-Saxon riddles); texts_793.json tatwine_05_membranis and others

history.text: King Eadberht of Kent frees a ship newly built at Minster in Thanet of all tribute and toll that his toll-gatherers take in the public places called Fordwic and Seorre. If she is wrecked, broken or worn out another may take her place, and what her people gain by trading they must faithfully offer to the king, with the ship, at Fordwic.
history.source: Sawyer 29 (763 or 764), the dossier's rendering: esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/29.html

history.text: Offa of Mercia rules Kent himself. Kent has no king of its own until he dies.
history.source: dossier 1 (list of the kings of Kent)

history.text: Offa frees the churches of Kent of their burdens, except service in Kent against pagan seamen with roving fleets.
Æthelheard, Offa's man, is enthroned as archbishop on 21 July by Hygberht, Offa's own archbishop of Lichfield. Offa's new heavy penny is being struck in the city.
Offa dies. Eadberht Præn, who had once been a priest, takes Kent, and the archbishop flees.
This year Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, wasted Kent and led Eadberht bound into Mercia. His brother Cuthred is made king of Kent.
On 12 October the council of Clofesho ends the archbishopric of Lichfield. Canterbury has its old rank again.
The nuns of Lyminge are given, as a refuge in need, six acres by Saint Mary's church in the west of the city, between the Stour and the city wall.
King Baldred is driven north over the Thames, and Kent turns to Ecgberht of Wessex.
This year the heathen men for the first time stay the winter on Thanet. Three hundred and fifty ships come into the mouth of the Thames, and the crews storm Canterbury and London.
A charter of the city is witnessed by Æthelstan 'and the inner townsmen' and by Æthelhelm 'and the cnihts' guild': the first guild named in England. Rats have since cut a hole in the leaf.
history.source: Sawyer 1199 (858 x 866) and its notes (dossier 2, 3, 7). The year is the start of the span, not a record

history.text: The heathen army sits on Thanet and takes Kent's promise of money. Under cover of the promise it steals inland by night and overruns all east Kent.

About these years a gospel book written in gold letters, probably made in Canterbury, is in a heathen army's hands. Ealdorman Alfred and his wife Wærburh buy it back with pure gold and give it to Christ Church.
history.source: the Old English note in the Stockholm Codex Aureus (dossier 7). The year is ours: the note gives none (?)

history.text: King Æthelstan's law gives Canterbury seven moneyers: four the king's, two the bishop's, one the abbot's.
history.source: chronicle_793.json (II Æthelstan, the Grately code); the division from the dossier's memory (dossier 4). The year is approximate (?)

history.text: This year King Edgar ordered all Thanet-land to be plundered.
The abbey of Saint Peter and Saint Paul outside the wall is dedicated anew, to Augustine as well, by Archbishop Dunstan.
Bruman the port-reeve is said to have given Abbot Sigeric two fenced plots and a meadow at Fordwic for his life, and then to the abbey. The year fits neither the abbot nor the reeve.
history.source: Sawyer 1654, dated by the abbey's late chroniclers; dossier 8 for the doubt (?)

history.text: Soon after Lammas Thorkell's army comes to Sandwich and turns at once on Canterbury. East Kent buys peace for three thousand pounds.

Between the Nativity of Saint Mary and Michaelmas the army besets Canterbury and takes it by treachery: Ælfmær betrayed it, whose life Archbishop Ælfheah had saved. The archbishop, Bishop Godwine, Abbess Leofrun and the king's reeve Ælfweard are taken.
On 19 April the army, drunk on wine brought from the south, kills Archbishop Ælfheah at Greenwich with the bones and horns of oxen.
In June King Cnut has Saint Ælfheah's body carried from London to Canterbury and laid on the north side of Christ's altar.
On 18 May Saint Mildred's body is brought from Thanet to Saint Augustine's, against fierce opposition on the island.
Cnut gives Christ Church the haven of Sandwich, as far inland as a man can throw a taper-axe from a ship afloat at the highest tide.
King Edward's writ gives Saint Augustine's as much land within Fordwic as he had: his two thirds of the borough. Earl Godwin had held the third.
history.source: Sawyer 1092 (1053 x 1066), the dossier's rendering; '1055' is Hasted's year (dossier 8)

history.text: Fordwic is a small borough of ninety-six house plots, paying thirteen shillings and worth a hundred.

eras.text: Offa's last years. The toll men are a Mercian king's and the pennies are his new heavy ones. The archbishop is his man, newly enthroned, and Kent does not love either of them. Frankish hulls are turned away; pilgrims still go out with letters from Christ Church.

Eadberht Præn's rising. The archbishop is gone, the moneyers cut dies for a king who was a priest, and the toll man is not sure whose toll he takes. In 798 the Mercian army wastes Kent; the track to the city is full of people going the other way.

Mercian Kent, ruined and then quiet. The archbishop comes home, goes to Rome and wins back his rank at Clofesho; after him Wulfred quarrels with the king over the minsters. Nuns from Lyminge keep a refuge inside the wall. The scribes are busy.

West Saxon Kent. A new king's name on the penny, the same moneyers at the benches. The books are still being written, in a worse hand each year, and there is talk at every landing of ships on Sheppey.

The heathen years. Canterbury is stormed in 851 and east Kent overrun in 865. Books are carried off for their covers and bought back with gold. The churches are short of men who can write Latin, and the landing sees more armed men than merchants.

The slow mending. The city is walled and watched, seven moneyers strike there by King Æthelstan's law, and under Dunstan the monks come back to their books. Fordwic is a row of plots where foreign merchants land for the two churches.

The raids again. Thanet is overrun, east Kent pays three thousand pounds, and in 1011 the city is taken by treachery and its archbishop led away. Every keel on the river is counted twice: once for the toll and once for the tribute.

Cnut's peace. The murdered archbishop comes home a saint, Saint Mildred is carried in from Thanet, Sandwich haven is given to Christ Church. Pilgrims come up the Stour with silver, and the toll man smiles.

King Edward's day. Fordwic is a small borough of ninety-six plots. The king gives his two thirds of it to Saint Augustine's, and from then the toll is the abbot's. Bruman the reeve takes the customs of foreign merchants, some of them unjustly.

sites.name: The hythe at the tide's end
sites.see: A low bank of trodden gravel on the south side of a brown river no wider than a long bowshot is far. Five or six boats lie stem to the bank, masts down, on a falling tide; beyond them reeds, alders and flat wet marsh to the edge of the sky. Behind, a line of hurdle fences and thatch. A heron stands where the last boat ends. Mud, cut reed, woodsmoke, and no sea smell at all.
sites.source: the river is tidal to Fordwich, its tidal limit (Tatton-Brown 1992); ships 'were moored' at the quay 'where all goods were laded and unladed' (Hasted 1800, of the later port). Where boats lay in 793 is not known (dossier 1, 8): the hythe is ours

sites.name: The king's toll place
sites.see: A bench under a lean-to of hurdles at the head of the hythe, with a peg-board behind it hung with tally sticks, one for each ship that has standing here. A heavy man with a white wand sits on the bench; beside him a clerk's boy holds a wax tablet he cannot read. Three ships have small wooden crosses painted on the board instead of sticks. Everything that lands walks between the bench and the river.
sites.source: the king's toll-gatherers (thelonearii) in the public place Fordwic: Sawyer 29 (763 or 764). The toll place has not been found (dossier 2); the bench, the board and the wand are ours. After Edward's writ the toll was the abbot's (Hasted vol. 9)

sites.name: The strand market
sites.see: Between the fences and the water, a strip of gravel where goods stand as they come off the boats: querns in straw, jars with their mouths tied, bales under hides. Women from the marsh farms sit with eggs, cheeses and live hens in withy cages; a monk's cart from the city waits with its ox unyoked. A buyer lifts a cloth to the light. Hens, wet straw, hot bread from somebody's oven.
sites.source: no cargo of Fordwic is listed; the Thanet nuns' crew deal in 'goods of various kinds' (Sawyer 29; dossier 4). Wine from the south (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1012), salt from Chislet marsh, querns and hops in the Graveney boat (dossier 4) are the region's record, not this strand's. No market day is known (dossier 8)

sites.name: The ale-house at the track's foot
sites.see: A long low house with its door to the track and its back to the river, a bush on a pole over the lintel. Inside, one hearth in the middle of the floor, smoke in the thatch, benches along the walls and a carter asleep with his whip across his knees. Boatmen sit on the river side and men from the city on the other. The ale is brown and thick, and the trout on the board is as long as a forearm.
sites.source: invented: an ale-house (say ale-house, BRIEF.md) at the foot of the track to the city. The host answers for a guest of three nights (Hlothhere and Eadric 15). The Stour's big trout were famous by 1653 (dossier 4)

sites.name: The ford to Sturry
sites.see: Upstream of the last boat the river spreads thin over gravel, and a line of stakes marks where a cart can cross at low water. On the far bank a few roofs, a smith's lean-to with a bed of charcoal glowing under it, and the road that runs on east to the Thanet ferry. A boy drives geese through the shallows. At high water the stakes stand in the stream to their middles and nobody crosses.
sites.source: the ford, later a bridge, to Sturry, and the Thanet road through Sturry to Sarre (dossier 1; no bridge before 1066, dossier 2). Hearths and slag at Sturry are of the sixth and seventh centuries (Kent HER, TR 16 SE 91): the smith of 793 is ours

sites.name: The fenced plots
sites.see: A row of narrow plots running back from the river, each inside its own fence of wattle and thorn: a house, a pit, a store raised on posts against the damp, a boat's ribs leaning on a wall. A gate stands open on one where a man is stacking hides under a thatch. A ditch runs straight down between two plots to the water. Dogs on ropes, a child with a stick counting bales aloud and getting it wrong.
sites.source: a reeve's two hagas (fenced plots) and a meadow at Fordwic (Sawyer 1654); ninety-six plots in 1066 (Domesday); a boundary or track running to the river, seen near the church in 2006 (Kent HER, TR 15 NE 1797). How many plots there were in 793 is not known (dossier 1)

sites.name: The mares' marsh
sites.see: East of the plots the land lies flat and green to a line of willows: wet meadow cut by black ditches, mares and foals standing in it to their hocks. A man with a long rake turns hay on the only dry ridge; behind him a farm on a low rise, a midden, a hen-run and a woman calling ten names. Plovers get up as you walk. Under a wide grey sky it smells of mint, dung and standing water.
sites.source: Stodmarsh is 'mare marsh', named beside Fordwic in 675 (Sawyer 7; dossier 1, 3); a meadow goes with the reeve's plots (Sawyer 1654). The farm wife and the hayward are the givers of the riddles in riddles_793.json (Exeter 13 and 34)

sites.name: Saint Martin's, where the track ends
sites.see: Two miles from the river the track climbs a little hill and stops at a small old church of red Roman tile and flint, older than anyone's grandfather can count. Its door stands open; inside it is narrow, dark and cool, with one lamp. From the churchyard the city lies below: a grey wall, thatch and smoke inside it, and outside it, nearer, the long roofs of the abbey. A boatman kneels with his cap in his hand.
sites.source: the track from Fordwich runs south-west to Saint Martin's church and the city, two miles (Hasted) or three (Tatton-Brown) (dossier 1, 6). A church of Saint Martin on the east side of the city, built while the Romans were in the island, where Queen Bertha prayed: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.26 (Jane 1903), from memory (?)

sites.name: The abbey of the kings' graves
sites.see: Outside the east wall, inside a bank and a gate of its own, two stone churches stand in a line with a paved yard between them. In the north side-chamber of the older one the first archbishops lie in a row; in the south, the kings of Kent. A porter with a bunch of keys looks at your shoes. Beyond the churches, a long room with shuttered windows where the books are kept and nobody raises his voice.
sites.source: the abbey outside the walls: two churches (613, about 624), a library and writing room, the graves of Kent's kings; Abbot Guthheard by its own tradition 787-803; renamed for Augustine in 978; Saint Mildred's body here from 1030 (dossier 2, 3, 5). The side-chambers from Bede II.3 and II.5, from memory (?)

sites.name: The wall and the east gate
sites.see: A Roman wall of flint with courses of red tile, patched with timber where it has fallen, and in it an arch wide enough for one cart. A man with a spear leans in its shade and asks nobody anything. Through the arch, a lane of fenced plots and thatch, pigs, a woman selling onions from a cloth. Carters shout for room. Whatever is news in Kent is said here first and loudest.
sites.source: the Roman wall and gates of Canterbury; 'the city wall' in the grant of the Lyminge refuge (Sawyer 160, 804); chapels over the gates and the cattle market outside the wall are later (dossier 2). The spearman and the onion seller are ours

sites.name: Christ Church and the writing room
sites.see: Inside the wall, the archbishop's church: stone, long and plain, with a porch on its south side where men wait with their caps off. Beside it a hall, and off the hall a room with a north light where four men sit at sloped boards with quills, and a fifth rules lines with a point. A calfskin is stretched on a frame by the door. Nobody looks up. It smells of gall ink, chalk and cold feet.
sites.source: the Saxon cathedral found under the nave in 1993, rebuilt larger in the ninth or tenth century and burnt in 1067 (dossier 2); the scribes of Christ Church (npc_roles_793.json, role scribe; riddles_793.json: Tatwine's riddles bought here). The room and its light are ours

sites.name: The moneyers' benches
sites.see: A lane off the market inside the wall, and in it three open-fronted sheds, each with a stump of oak set in the floor and a die standing in the stump. A man holds a second die over a blank of silver; another swings the hammer; a boy sweeps the floor with a hare's foot and tips the dust into a dish. Scales no bigger than a hand hang in a wooden case. Each blow rings like a small bell.
sites.source: coin is struck in Canterbury for kings and archbishops; none is known at Fordwic (dossier 2, 4, 8). Offa's heavy penny from 792/3; pennies of about 822-824 naming only the moneyer and 'Dorobernia civitas'; seven moneyers by Æthelstan's law (dossier 4). The sheds are ours

people.name: Æthelheard
people.trait: Offa's man in a Kentish see, and the Kentish know it: learned, cautious, in exile when Kent rises.
people.want: Canterbury's old rank made whole against Offa's new archbishop at Lichfield; a safe crossing to Rome.
people.voice: Measured; says 'the king' and means the Mercian one.
people.looks: About fifty, tonsured, the pallium over a dark vestment, a crozier, a train of clerks with a book chest; on the road a plain travelling cloak and a mule.
knows: who is king in Kent and how long he is likely to stay so
what the two churches of the city are buying this season: wax, wine, oil, calfskin
who at Rome, at Tours and at the Frankish court will read a letter from Canterbury
which pilgrims went out with his letter and which were refused one
that he is out of Kent from 796 to 798 and at Rome from 801 to 803: a clerk speaks for him then

ties.note: the same person
Alcuin writes to him in his flight and tells him to go back to his flock

the abbot at the Canche lets his pilgrims through, and counts them

the moneyer who strikes the archbishop's pennies in the lane, with the king's name on the other side; he asks Eoba, lightly, whose name he would leave off first
a priest of Saint Paul's who carries his letters between the Thames and the Kentish shore, and prays for him by name while he is out of Kent
the old bishop of the East Angles owes Canterbury his obedience and gives it, without liking the king it comes through
took his written oath in 798, the first leaf he read on coming home to Kent; he asked a clerk where Dommoc was, and was ashamed of asking
the nun who keeps the Thanet minster's ships: he sends for one when he must cross water without being counted
the ferryman of the Wantsum carried his people over at night in 796 and was paid in a blessing
the reeve at Dofras is Offa's man in Kent as he is, and the only layman who says so to him kindly
the priest of the shore church at Hamwic, who found a ship for the bishop of Winchester's men when they went to Rome with him (?)
the guest master of Saint Josse lodged him on the road to Rome and found him a mule
a mass-priest by the ford at Gipeswic whom he has never seen: the letters come by the bishop of Dommoc, dated by saints, and he answers them (?)
the toll man at the Wantsum crossing let his people pass in 796 and did not ask which way they went; he has not forgotten whose man that was
King Coenwulf's daughter was a girl at her father's court in his day: it is his successor Wulfred who will have to fight her for Reculver and Minster

lines.greet: A Frisian at Christ Church has come either for the scribes or for me. If it is for me, say it shortly, because I have a great deal to read.
lines.greet_again: You are the merchant from the Rhine mouth. Sit down and tell me what the Franks' king has said of our king, and I will tell you what you may land.
rumour: The king has made a second archbishop at Lichfield. I received my seat from that man's hands. You will understand that I do not speak of it.
A true pilgrim crosses free, by the Frankish king's word. I write the letters for them, but I cannot write what is in a man's bundle.
Master Alcuin writes that a shepherd does not leave his flock. Master Alcuin writes from Tours, where nobody has yet tried to kill him.
lines.saying: A see is older than any king who gives it. I remind myself of that most mornings.
lines.trusted: You carried what was the church's and asked no fee. There is a seat for you here, and a letter to anyone you name.
lines.returned: Kent is quiet because it is ruined, and so I prayed for the one and was given the other. What do you bring?
lines.farewell: Go down with the ebb. If the reeve at the hythe asks whose wax that was, it was mine.

people.source: spine.json cast.aethelheard, the same facts. Chosen in 792, enthroned 21 July 793 by Hygberht of Lichfield; fled Kent 796-798; at Rome 801-803; died 12 May 805 (dossier 1, 3, 5; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). His birth year, manner and words are ours (?). Alcuin's letter to him in his flight: MGH Epistolae IV, through the spine (?)

people.name: Tilred
people.trait: The king's reeve and toll-gatherer at the landing: Kentish born, serving his third king, and never once heard to say which of them he liked.
people.want: The toll counted right, his tallies believed in the city, and his daughter married to a moneyer's son and not to a boatman.
people.fear: A charter he cannot read being waved at him; a king's man from Mercia asking to see the tallies of two years ago.
people.voice: Slow and exact. Counts on his fingers where you can see. Answers a question with the law, then with what is really done.
people.looks: Mid forties in 793, heavy, bald on top with a brown beard going grey, a russet cloak pinned at the shoulder with a disc brooch, a white wand and a bundle of tally sticks.
knows: the toll on your ship, which is by the ship and not by the cargo, and which three ships owe none
who must witness a sale for it to stand, and who will
what the archbishop's household and the abbey are buying, a week before the carts come down
the state of the river: where the last reach has silted, and which tide will float you
who came down the track from the city today, and in what temper

ties.note: Dunwalh at Sarre takes the same king's toll; they send each other the count of the abbess's ships and it never agrees
sends him word of what the archbishop's household is buying
the wic-reeve of Lundenwic looks over the Kentish tallies for the king once a year
tolls the church's goods and is told each time that they are God's
three seasons of eggs and a cheese, on a tally she keeps and he does not dispute
wants his daughter married to the moneyer's son; brings Eoba every strange coin taken at the hythe
by the old king's word her ship's gains are to be offered to the king here, and she has her own idea of what was gained
the hayward keeps the meadow that goes with the reeve's plots; the reeve counts the hay and is told, in one sentence, that it is all there

lines.greet: You lie at the king's hythe, so you pay the king's toll, and it is by the ship. I will look at her and not in her, unless you give me cause.
lines.greet_again: Your stick is on the board, the third from the door. The river has dropped a hand since you were here, so go out on the big tide.
rumour: The Franks have shut their shores to us, and we ours to them. A Frisian is not a Frank, or so I have decided, though the wic-reeve has not.
The abbess's ship pays nothing here, by the old king's word, but she must show me what she earns. She shows me very little, and shows it beautifully.
The clerks sell riddles, and one of the old archbishop's, answered to my face, passes a ship free. It is a custom, and you need not ask who began it.
lines.saying: It is two miles to the city by the track, and three if the man is carrying your goods.
lines.trusted: I will tell you what the cellarer wants before the cellarer knows. Bring wax by Candlemas and name your price.
lines.farewell: The ebb is in an hour. Mind the stakes below the alders, because I have pulled better boats than yours off them.

people.source: invented. The office is the king's toll-gatherer of Sawyer 29 and the reeve who witnesses a sale (Hlothhere and Eadric 16); nobody of Fordwic is named in 793 (dossier 3, 8). The riddle that frees a ship is the game's own (riddles_793.json rw_toll_fordwic). His saying turns the two measures of the track, two miles in Hasted and three in Tatton-Brown

people.name: Eadhun
people.trait: A scribe of Christ Church with the best hand in the room and the worst eyes: fond of riddles, short of patience, and always cold.
people.want: Good calfskin, a window that faces south, and one book in his life written in gold.
people.fear: Fire in the writing room; his eyes going before the psalter is finished; a book of his under a heathen's knife for its cover.
people.voice: Dry and quick. Complains first, then helps. Sets a riddle the way other men clear their throats.
people.looks: Not yet thirty in 793, thin, stooped, tonsured, ink to the second knuckle of the right hand, a patched black habit, a penknife and a quill behind his ear.
knows: what a book is worth, skin by skin and month by month, and who will pay it
Archbishop Tatwine's forty riddles, and which leaves of them can be bought
who has borrowed a book from Christ Church and not sent it back
what is written in any charter you bring him, and whether it is what you were told
which pilgrims' letters he wrote this month

ties.note: writes the archbishop's letters and the pilgrims' passes, and is corrected in red
lent the canon of Saint Martin's a psalter to copy, and wants it back
the Northumbrian who carries Alcuin's letters; each tries to borrow a book off the other
learned his riddling from a leaf of Alcuin's questions for the king's son, copied at third hand
draws the letters the moneyer cuts into his dies, and is paid in clipped silver for gilding
copies the Thanet minster's charters for her, so there is one where the damp cannot reach it
she sells him the whites of eggs for his gilding and tells him he wants feeding
the priest of Saint Paul's who misses his books: each has been trying to borrow one off the other for ten years
the priest of the shore church at Hamwic has Aldhelm by heart: a leaf of Tatwine goes west for a leaf of Aldhelm written fair
wrote out the form of the East Angles' bishop's oath for him, and is owed wax for it (?)
after his day: the leaf on which Dommoc's last bishop swears his obedience is kept in this room, by the pupils of his pupils (?)

lines.greet: Shut the door, because the wind is on my neck. You want a leaf, or a letter read, or a book carried, so tell me which, since I have lost the light already.
lines.greet_again: So it is you again, and still with no calfskin. A book is a herd of calves, merchant, so bring me the herd and I will show you the book.
rumour: A canon at Dofras has had our psalter since the feast of Saint Martin. If you lie there, tell him the saint is watching.
The old archbishop made forty riddles, and somebody else made sixty to round out the hundred. The forty are better, though I may be partial.
When the heathen take a book they keep the cover and throw the words in the sea. I think of that when the ink will not flow.
lines.saying: Three fingers hold the pen, and the whole back pays for it.
lines.trusted: This one is the sword and its house. Answer it at the hythe, to the reeve's face, and see what he does with your tally.
lines.teaches: Count the skins, count the months, weigh the gold. Now you know what a heathen has in his hand and he does not.
lines.farewell: Go on, and mind the skin by the door, because it is not dry, and shut the door behind you.

people.source: invented. The scribe of Christ Church is the role's own example (npc_roles_793.json) and the seller of Tatwine's riddles (riddles_793.json; unlocks_793.json text.tatwine_05_membranis, 15, 30). His saying is the common scribes' colophon, 'three fingers write, the whole body labours', in our words. A real scribe of the house, Eadui Basan, is two centuries later (dossier 3)

people.name: Eoba
people.trait: A moneyer of Canterbury who has put his name on pennies for a king and for a queen, and expects to outlast both.
people.want: Good silver, clean dies, and never again to be told to make the penny heavier in the middle of a year.
people.fear: Striking for the wrong king. A moneyer's name is on every coin, and a coin lasts longer than a pardon.
people.voice: Flat and good-humoured. Talks of kings as customers. Bites nothing: he listens to a coin ring.
people.looks: About fifty, short and thick in the arms, burn scars on both hands, a leather apron over a good green tunic, a small balance in a case hung at his neck.
knows: what the king's new heavy penny weighs and what an old light one is worth against it
what he gives for Frankish deniers, cut silver and old small thick pennies, and the loss
whose name is on the dies this month
that Ibba strikes at Lundenwic, and what he thinks of Ibba's lettering
what a gold piece with marks nobody can read is likely to be

ties.note: Ibba signs for the same king up the Thames; each says the other's pennies are a grain light
the reeve brings him every strange coin from the hythe, and a daughter he would like married
Eadhun draws his letters; Eoba pays in clippings for the scribe's gilding
the archbishop's pennies are struck in the same lane, with the king's name on the other side
the wic-reeve carries the king's word on weight and dies from Lundenwic
the East Angles' moneyer, who has put three kings' names on the same silver: they agree by letter that kings are customers (?)

lines.greet: If that is Frankish silver, put it on the cloth. I will give you the king's new pennies for it, less my share and the fire's, and the fire is the greedier of the two.
lines.greet_again: Here is the Frisian with the honest deniers. The pennies are heavier this year, so there are fewer of them, and you need not look at me like that, because I only hold the die.
rumour: I struck for the queen, with her face on the coin. No other moneyer in England has done that, though no other queen has asked.
A pilgrim showed me gold with marks on it like worm tracks. They say that Ibba at Lundenwic copied one, but I would not copy what I cannot read.
When a king dies I keep the old dies under the bench for a season. You would be surprised how often a season is enough.
lines.saying: A king's name is soft work. It is the cross on the back that wears out the die.
lines.trusted: Bring me your strange silver first and unweighed. I will tell you what it is, and take a twentieth instead of a tenth.
lines.farewell: Count them at my bench, not at your boat. Once they leave the lane they are yours, light or not.

people.source: Eoba is a moneyer named on Canterbury pennies of Offa and of his queen Cynethryth (dossier 3; lundenwic.json for Ibba). That he also struck for Eadberht Præn and Coenwulf is from memory (?). Nothing else is known of him: his age, years, manner and ties are invented. The heavy penny of 792/3: dossier 4

people.name: Cwengyth
people.trait: A farm wife of the marsh edge who sells eggs, cheese and hens on the strand, remembers every face that ever bought from her, and what it paid.
people.want: A dry year, a fox-proof hen-run, and her son kept off the boats.
people.fear: The winter flood coming over the ridge; an army of any king eating its way across the marsh.
people.voice: Loud, warm and exact about pennies. Calls every boatman 'child'. Asks after your crew by name, and gets the names right.
people.looks: Mid thirties in 793, broad and red-armed, a linen head-cloth, a brown gown kilted for the mud, a withy cage of hens on one hip and a basket on the other.
knows: the price of eggs, cheese, butter and a live hen, here and inside the wall
whose mares are on the marsh and who is selling a foal
everything said at the hythe since the last tide
when the river will flood, by the plovers
a riddle about ten chickens, which she tells to anybody who buys twice

ties.note: her brother, the hayward; she feeds him and he mends her fences
he owes her: three seasons of eggs on a tally stick she keeps in the rafters
Tidburh at the Sarre crossing is her mother's sister's daughter; they send each other cheeses and gossip by the carters
sells him the white of eggs for his gilding and tells him he needs feeding

lines.greet: I have eggs, child, laid this morning, and a cheese that will see you to the Franks' shore. You are thin, because they do not feed you on that boat.
lines.greet_again: There he is! Are there four of you still, and the big quiet one among them? That is good. I kept the brown hen's eggs back, because I said that you would come on the tide.
rumour: The reeve has owed me for eggs since the old king's day, and I keep the stick. One of us will die first, and I mean it to be him.
The clerks pay for egg white and throw away the yolk, which they say is for gilding. I have six children fed on what Christ Church throws away.
My cousin at the Sarre crossing says that four ships passed with crosses on them, and the abbess has three. Either somebody cannot count, or somebody can.
lines.saying: It is a good year when the dog gives to the raven.
lines.trusted: There were ten of them in the yard with their coats hung on the wall, child, so what was it that walked out? Guess it, and the cheese is yours.
lines.heir: You have your father's way of standing, and he owed me for a hen. No, sit down, because I am only teasing you, and it was two hens.
lines.farewell: Go safely, and bring me back a Frankish jar with a lid, and your whole crew with it.

people.source: invented. She is the farm wife who gives Exeter riddle 13 at Fordwic (riddles_793.json; unlocks_793.json text.exeter_13_ten_chickens). Her saying is one of the Durham Proverbs, about 1050, in the rendering of Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.md

people.name: Wicga
people.trait: The hayward of the marsh meadow: keeps the fences and the ditches, knows every mare by her walk, and says about one sentence a day.
people.want: The hay in dry; nobody's cattle in the meadow before Lammas; to be left alone with his rake.
people.fear: Strangers off the track. He has the old law by heart and a horn on his belt to remind them of it.
people.voice: Almost none. A grunt, a pointed rake, then one long slow sentence that turns out to be worth the wait.
people.looks: Past forty, tall, lean, burnt dark by the wind, a hooded cape of undyed wool, bare shins, a long wooden rake and a cow's horn on a thong.
knows: where the marsh will bear a man and where it will not
whose mares and foals are for sale, and which are sound
who left the track this week without sounding a horn
the weather for three days, from the ditch water and the plovers
a riddle about a thing with many teeth that feeds the cattle

ties.note: his sister; she talks for both of them
the meadow goes with the reeve's plots, and the reeve counts the hay
sells Dudda at the crossing a foal now and then and listens to him the whole way to Sarre

lines.greet: The track is over there and you are standing here, so you can blow a horn or go back to it.
lines.greet_again: You are the Frisian, and you should mind the ditch.
rumour: A stranger off the track, no shout, no horn: the old king's law says thief. I say it too, but I look first.
The grey mare's foal is sound, but the reeve's bay is not, whatever he tells you, as you will see if you look at the off hind.
lines.saying: 'Now it is up to the pig,' said the farmer sitting on the boar's back.
lines.trusted: It noses the ground and has more teeth than a hound, yet it bites nothing, and it feeds my beasts all winter, and I am holding it now.
lines.farewell: There will be rain by the second tide, so you should go now.

people.source: invented. He is the hayward who gives Exeter riddle 34 at Fordwic (riddles_793.json; unlocks_793.json text.exeter_34_rake); the role table has no hayward, so he stands as a farmer. The law of the stranger off the track is Wihtred's (695; dossier 6). His saying is one of the Durham Proverbs, in the rendering of Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.md

people.name: Alfred
people.trait: An ealdorman with land in Kent and Surrey, rich, plain-spoken and devout, who would sooner pay for a holy thing than fight for it and has done both.
people.want: The gold-lettered gospels out of heathen hands and on Christ's altar, with his name, his wife's and his daughter's written in them to be prayed for.
people.fear: Dying with the book still in the army's baggage; a go-between who talks.
people.voice: Blunt, a soldier's. Names a weight of gold before he names anything else, and waits to see whether you blink.
people.looks: About forty in 865, grey at the temples, a short cloak of good blue wool with a silver-gilt brooch, a sword he does not take off, his wife Wærburh beside him with a purse.
knows: where the army lies this season and who in it sells what it has taken
what the gospel book looks like: purple leaves and white, letters in gold and silver
what pure gold is worth against pennies, to the grain
which of Kent's men have paid the army and which have only promised
that the goldsmith Wulfhelm can tell at a glance whether a cover has been cut

ties.note: the reeve up the Thames hears first which of the army's men are selling; our tie, not a recorded one (?)
learned his trade of war as a young man under the ealdorman who took nine ships at Sandwich; our tie (?)
none recorded: the port-reeve of King Edward's day is given a far descent from Alfred's household in the game only (?)

lines.greet: You go among the heathen and come back again, which is good, because I want one thing bought from them, and I pay in pure gold. Do you blink at that?
lines.greet_again: Here is the merchant. Have you seen it, with its purple leaves and gold letters? Do not tell me what they asked for it, but tell me who was asking.
rumour: They made peace with Kent for a promise of money, and under the promise they rode out by night. I do not promise them anything, I weigh and I pay.
They do not want the book, they want its weight, so I will give them more than its weight and have the words too.
lines.saying: A holy book should not lie one night longer among men who cannot read it.
lines.trusted: My wife holds the gold, and she says that you have an honest face. She has been wrong about a face once, and she married him.
lines.farewell: Go by Thanet, and speak to one man only. If you are asked whose gold it is, it is God's.

people.source: Ealdorman Alfred and his wife Wærburh, who bought the gold-lettered gospel book 'from the heathen army' with pure gold and gave it to Christ Church: the Old English note in the Stockholm Codex Aureus, which names their daughter and a goldsmith Wulfhelm (dossier 3, 7). His will survives; his years here (865-888), his birth, his manner and his words are ours (?)

people.name: Bruman
people.trait: The port-reeve of King Edward's day: takes the customs of foreign merchants on the two churches' land in the city, and takes them with both hands.
people.want: The toll his, the abbot content, the archbishop's men kept guessing, and a grave inside the abbey wall paid for in advance.
people.fear: Being put to his oath before the shire about what he took and from whom.
people.voice: Hearty, a good host's. Remembers your father's name and your last cargo. The sum is always a little more than last time.
people.looks: About forty in 1045, stout, clean-shaven with a long moustache, a fur-edged cloak, rings on two fingers, a staff of office and a purse he keeps a hand on.
knows: what a foreign keel owes here and in the city, and what it can be made to owe
which plots at Fordwic are the abbot's, which the earl's, and which can be had
who the king's writ greets in Kent: the archbishop, the earl, the abbot, the sheriff
what Christ Church has at Sandwich haven, to the throw of an axe
which merchants of Rouen and Flanders are on the river this week

ties.note: the Dofras burgesses cross free of toll through all England; Bruman tolls them anyway and gives it back, slowly
the earl has the third penny of Fordwic until his death at Easter 1053
Wulfgar, the king's port-reeve in London: they compare what the men of Rouen paid at each landing, and it is never the same
claims it, in the game only: an ealdorman's blood is good for a reeve's standing (?)

lines.greet: A keel from over the sea is always welcome! You lie on the abbot's land now, by the king's gift, so you pay the abbot, and you pay him through me.
lines.greet_again: I knew your father's stem before I saw your face. The customs have gone up a little, as everything has, but sit down and drink first.
rumour: The king has given his two parts of this borough to Saint Augustine. The earl had the third. Nobody has told me yet whose man that makes me.
Christ Church holds Sandwich as far inland as a man can throw a small axe from a ship at the top of the tide. They chose a tall man.
lines.saying: There are ninety-six plots, with thirteen shillings to the king, and a hundred to whoever counts them.
lines.trusted: Between us: some of what I took from your house I took unjustly. I may yet have to swear to it. Better I give it back first.
lines.farewell: Go with God and the ebb, and tell them at Rouen that Bruman is a fair man. Say it twice, because they will not believe it once.

people.source: Bruman, port-reeve: his gift of two hagas and a meadow at Fordwic to Abbot Sigeric (Sawyer 1654, dated 991 by the abbey's late chroniclers); Domesday's reeve Bruman, in the time of King Edward, took the customs of foreign merchants on the two churches' land and later swore he had taken them unjustly (dossier 3, 8). We follow Domesday's date. His birth, looks, manner and words are ours (?)

stories.title: The sword and its house
stories.summary: The scribes of Christ Church sell Archbishop Tatwine's riddles by the leaf, and by a custom nobody admits to starting, one of them answered to the reeve's face passes a ship free of toll at the hythe. The leaf is in Latin, the reeve cannot read it, and the answer has to be the merchant's own.
stories.picture: The toll bench at the head of the hythe on a bright morning: a heavy bald reeve with a white wand holding a leaf of parchment upside down, a merchant before him with one hand raised as if weighing a thought, a thin inky monk watching from the track with his arms folded.

beats.text: Eadhun sells a leaf for fourteen pennies: thirty lines down, a thing that guards its master and is itself kept in a house it does not own. He will read it out once. He will not say the answer, and he wants to hear yours when you have it.
A clerk's boy offers the answer for two pennies and a cup. The carter beside him says the reeve knows a bought answer by the way it is said, and has a second question ready for those.

Tilred hears the answer with the leaf in his hand, the wrong way up. If it is right he takes your tally stick off the board and hangs a blank one. If it was bought he asks what the thing's house is made of.
The king's toll-reeve at Lundenwic has heard of the Fordwic custom and will not be outdone. He has a riddle of his own, of snow and ice, and the same freedom for the same wit.
The cathedral schoolmaster at Traiectum knows Tatwine by name and asks to copy the leaf. In return he opens his own: a riddle about a key.
The priest of the shore church at Hamwic has Aldhelm by heart and no Tatwine at all. He will give two riddles for the one leaf, and asks whether the Kentish reeve has ever been answered in Latin.
Abbot Lull at Dommoc gives a letter of greeting to masters who have answered his three. Shown at Christ Church, it gets a second leaf looked out without the asking.

endings.how: Read the leaf, or had it read aboard, and answered it yourself before the reeve.
endings.text: The blank stick hangs on the board for as long as Tilred is reeve. Eadhun hears of it by evening and sends down a second leaf, harder, with no price on it.
endings.reward: rw_toll_fordwic: toll none on your ship at Fordwic for some years; give_riddle of a second Tatwine leaf (riddle_tatwine_05_membranis); Eadhun friendly and Tilred amused; the flag fordwic_riddle_answered.

endings.how: Paid the clerk's boy for the answer and said it to the reeve.
endings.text: Tilred asks his second question and waits. Then he hangs your stick back where it was, a little higher, where he can see it from the bench.
endings.reward: Nothing off the toll; the leaf stays in the chest and can be tried again honestly after a year; Tilred cool for a season; the flag fordwic_riddle_bought.

endings.how: Carried the leaf to Traiectum and let the schoolmaster copy it.
endings.text: Tatwine's sword is read in a school on the Rhine. The schoolmaster's key comes back with you, and Eadhun, told of it, says a riddle that travels is a riddle that is alive.
endings.reward: give_riddle riddle_symphosius_04_clavis; standing with the school at Traiectum; Eadhun a friend, and copy_text at Christ Church at half the fee.

stories.reward: A ship free of toll at Fordwic, or the next leaf of the riddle road, and a scribe who looks up when you come in.

stories.title: A herd of calves
stories.summary: Eadhun the scribe will teach a merchant what a book is worth, if the merchant will bring him the skins to make one. Seventy years on the lesson is wanted: a gospel book in gold letters lies in a heathen army's baggage, and Ealdorman Alfred will pay pure gold to the man who can find it, price it and bring it home whole.
stories.picture: A dim tent of sailcloth on a chalk shore at dusk: a great book lying open on a sea chest, its leaves purple and white with gold letters catching a rushlight, a Northman's hand flat on one page and a merchant's small folding scale set down on the other.

beats.text: Eadhun wants calfskin: thirty good skins, unscarred, before the winter. He pays the church's price, which is fair and slow, and for the man who brings them he counts aloud what a gospel book costs in calves, months and gold.
Wicga knows who has calves and who has only promises. The skins of the marsh are thin and fine. He names a farm, and a price, and then says nothing for the rest of the walk.
The new bishop at Dommoc has a letter from Alcuin and no library. He asks what books a see ought to have and what they cost. A merchant taught at Christ Church can tell him, to the calf.

Ealdorman Alfred stops you in the arch. The gospels with the gold letters are gone from Christ's altar, and the army on Thanet has them. He names a weight of gold. His wife holds the purse and watches your face.

On the island a man of the army shows the book across a sea chest. He has priced it by its weight. A merchant who was taught at Christ Church knows the cover is the least of it, and has to choose whether to say so.
If the book was not bought on Thanet it comes to the Thames with the army's winter camp. A dealer has it now, and the price has learned to read.
The book is laid on the altar. A clerk writes above and below the first words of Matthew, in English, who bought it back and why. He asks how your name is spelled, and whether you want it there.

endings.how: Bought the book whole with the ealdorman's gold and carried it up the track to Christ Church.
endings.text: It lies on the altar for the love of God and the good of three souls, and no leaf is missing. The clerks pray for the ealdorman, his wife and their daughter by name, and for a merchant without one.
endings.reward: Alfred a fast friend, and through him a welcome at every hall in Kent and Surrey for the house's life; a tenth of the gold's weight in silver for the carrying; the flag bk_carried; act:copy_text free at Christ Church for this merchant and the next heir.

endings.how: Let the seller keep his own price, by weight, and said nothing of what the leaves were worth.
endings.text: He takes the gold for the cover and throws in the words, pleased with his bargain. You bring home a book in its bare boards. Alfred pays, looks at the boards, and has a goldsmith sent for.
endings.reward: The same friend, a little cooler, and the difference in gold in your own purse: a great sum (about two pounds of pennies (?)); the flag bk_carried; Wærburh never quite meets your eye.

endings.how: Bought it with your own silver and sold it to a Frankish church.
endings.text: A bishop over the water has a gospel book with gold letters and does not ask where the English note in it would have gone. At Canterbury the place on the altar stays empty, and the ealdorman knows who went to Thanet.
endings.reward: The best single sale of a generation (silver, very much); the flag bk_knows_worth kept and bk_lost set; Kent's halls shut to the house while Alfred lives, and the scribes of Christ Church sell this house no leaf for a generation.

endings.how: Never brought Eadhun his calfskin, and went to Thanet unable to price a book.
endings.text: You pay what is asked or you do not. The man of the army laughs at the scale. The book comes home or it goes to the Thames, and either way the profit is somebody else's.
endings.reward: The carrier's fee only, if it is bought; the lesson can still be had from a later scribe for a herd of calves.

stories.reward: The flag bk_knows_worth from the first half (a scribe has taught you what a book is worth, and to whom), a standing order for calfskin at Christ Church (bk_parchment), and in the heir's time an ealdorman's friendship or a bishop's silver.

stories.title: Whose name on the penny
stories.summary: In five years the moneyers of Canterbury cut dies for Offa, for his queen, for a priest who made himself king of Kent, and for the Mercian who led that king away in chains. A merchant who holds the wrong king's silver on the wrong morning finds out what a name is worth; one who listens to Eoba finds out a day sooner.
stories.picture: The moneyers' lane inside the wall: a thick-armed man in a leather apron holding up a new penny between finger and thumb to a merchant, an oak stump with a die in it between them, and under the bench, half hidden by a cloth, a row of older dies.

beats.text: The king's penny is heavier this year, by his order. Eoba changes Frankish deniers and old light pennies into new ones at a loss he names before he touches them. He mentions that he keeps old dies under the bench.

Offa is dead and Kent has a king of its own, a man who was once a priest. Tilred takes the toll in whatever is offered and writes the king's name on no tally. New pennies with the new name are in the market by Martinmas.
Eoba will change Offa's pennies for Eadberht's at par, today. He does not say what he will do next year. He asks, as one asks about weather, which name the wic-reeve at Lundenwic is taking.
Ibba strikes for the Mercian king and takes Kentish pennies of the priest-king as cut silver, by weight, at a loss. He says Eoba's letters were always better than his loyalty.
Dunwalh at Sarre takes the toll in whatever is offered and says 'the king' as he always has. Asked which king, he says the one whose pennies you are holding.
At Dofras the old reeve's bench has a new man on it, who pays in the new king's pennies a third over the rate and asks nobody to take them twice.
Kent is wasted and Eadberht is led bound into Mercia. His pennies are silver and nothing more. Eoba, who is still at his bench, melts them without comment and offers a cup to anyone who held many.
In a later moneyer's day the pennies carry no king's name at all: only the moneyer's and the city's. Nobody at the benches is sure whose turn it is, and nobody wants to be first to guess.

endings.how: Kept in with Eoba, brought him your strange silver first, and changed out of Eadberht's pennies when he asked about the weather.
endings.text: You hold the Mercian king's coin on the morning the Mercian army comes. Eoba nods across the lane. From then he takes your word on foreign silver and half his usual share.
endings.reward: The unlock fordwic.unlock.eobas_bench (change_coin at Canterbury at half the loss, inherited once); Eoba a fast friend; a price word each call on which silver is passing where.

endings.how: Took the new king's pennies gladly and traded in them through the rising.
endings.text: For two years you are a friend of Kent, well served at the hythe and inside the wall. In the third your chest is full of a bound man's name. It melts down to about four parts in five.
endings.reward: Standing with the Kentish 796-798 and cheap goods in the rising; then a loss of a fifth on the silver held; Eoba friendly all the same, since he made them.

endings.how: Trusted no name and took everything by weight on your own scale.
endings.text: You lose a little on every sale and nothing on any morning. The moneyers think you a hard man and a foreigner. Tilred thinks you the only sensible one on the river.
endings.reward: No loss at either change of king; the flag sv_scale honoured here (nobody shorts you at Fordwic); Tilred friendly; no bench of your own in the lane.

stories.reward: A moneyer who takes your word, or two fat years and a lean morning, or a name on the river for a man who weighs: and the lesson, for the heir, of the pennies of 822 that named no king at all.

stories.title: What is in a man's bundle
stories.summary: While the two kings keep their shores shut, the only English who cross freely are pilgrims, and a pilgrim is a man with a letter from Christ Church. Eadhun writes them, the archbishop seals them, and a cloth dealer from the city wants one very much. What a skipper says here is carried down the river to Sarre and over the sea to the abbot's toll men.
stories.picture: The south porch of Christ Church in grey morning light: three men with staffs and wallets waiting their turn, one of them in a better cloak than a pilgrim should own with a tight bundle between his feet, and through the open door a thin monk at a board, writing, not looking up.

beats.text: Three wait in the porch for letters of passage to Rome. Eadhun writes two without looking up. At the third he asks what a man bound for the Apostles wants with twelve cloaks, and looks at you for the answer.
The scribe will not write the third letter until a skipper says what the man is. A plain word either way is enough, and is remembered in the porch, at the hythe and over the water.

The third man buys your ale. He has cloth the Franks would pay double for in a shut year and no way to land it. A skipper's word to the scribe that he is known and pious would be worth a fifth of the sale.

Tilred says what the law is: the ports are shut to traders and open to pilgrims, and it is not the reeve's work to see into a man's soul. He would like to know, all the same, before the wic-reeve asks him.

Three for the thresholds of the Apostles wait at the crossing with letters in a Christ Church hand. The ferryman has carried their bundle and winks. Whether there are three letters or two was settled at Fordwic.

On the shingle at Dofras nine wait where three waited at Sarre, and the letters in their wallets are in the same Christ Church hand. The clerk of Saint Martin's says he can read which were written gladly.

The abbot's toll men pass true pilgrims free and open bundles when a skipper looks sideways. A letter from Canterbury on a cloth dealer is a thing the abbot will write to the archbishop about, by name.
King Charles's letter is read: true pilgrims free, traders to pay the toll, and men who mix the two to be dealt with. Æthelheard asks his scribe how many letters went out, and to whom.

endings.how: Told the scribe plainly that you did not know the man.
endings.text: Two letters go out. The cloth dealer walks to Sarre without one and tries his luck. When the Frankish king's complaint is read, the archbishop's count is clean, and he knows whose plain word kept it so.
endings.reward: Æthelheard and Eadhun friendly; the flag bs_ban_heard; a letter of passage in your own name for one voyage to a Frankish port while the ban stands; a cloth dealer in the city who will not sell to you.

endings.how: Vouched for him, and took a fifth.
endings.text: Three letters go out and the cloaks sell well. In 796 the abbot writes, the archbishop asks his scribe, and Eadhun says whose word he took. You are not asked in to explain.
endings.reward: Silver, a fair voyage's worth; a partner in English cloth while the ports are shut; the archbishop's door cool to the house until he dies, and the pilgrims' letters refused to anyone you carry.

endings.how: Told Tilred what was in the bundle before the wic-reeve asked.
endings.text: The cloaks pay the king's toll at the hythe and go nowhere. Tilred has something to show Lundenwic for once. The two true pilgrims cross with you, and pray for you because nobody told them.
endings.reward: Tilred a fast friend and a season's toll forgiven; standing with the wic-reeve Wighelm; the deed of carrying pilgrims; one enemy inside the wall.

endings.how: Drank his ale and said nothing to anybody.
endings.text: The matter goes on without you. You hear how it came out at Sarre, from the ferryman, at length.
endings.reward: Nothing lost; the ale was free.

stories.reward: The archbishop's trust and a letter of your own, or cloth silver and a cold porch, or a reeve who owes you: and the same three men met again at Sarre and at the Canche, where what was settled here is remembered.

stories.title: He who was England's head
stories.summary: In 1009 east Kent buys Thorkell's army off for three thousand pounds; two years later the city is taken by treachery and the archbishop led away, and in 1012 he is killed by drunken men who had wine from the south. A merchant with a keel on the Stour is asked to pay a share, to carry people out, and to sell wine, in that order.
stories.picture: The hythe at night under a red glow to the south-west where the city is: people crowding down the bank into a merchant's boat with bundles and a child, a nun among them, the reeve holding the stern line and looking back up the track.

beats.text: A bishop of Winchester rides down among the tilts at Hamtun to fetch a Northman king to the English king and his confirming. He is Ælfheah, who will sit at Canterbury; the men who carry his word to the ships now will be known to him then.

Soon after Lammas the army is at Sandwich. East Kent will pay three thousand pounds and every plot, keel and plough is assessed. The reeve reads out the house's share. It is large, and it is asked politely, once.
The same reckoning is laid out on a cloth before Saint Martin's at Dofras. What Fordwic's keels pay and what Dofras's boats pay go to the fleet at Sandwich in one chest.

Archbishop Ælfheah will not let the church's tenants be squeezed for his own safety. He asks whether your keel could take the books and the relics down the river, if it came to it, and where a Frisian would hide them.

Between the Nativity of Saint Mary and Michaelmas the city is beset. Then one night the sky over the track is red and people are on the bank: monks, women, a nun of Thanet. A man they trusted opened a gate. The ebb is in an hour.

Those you carried are landed on Thanet or taken on to the Thames. The army's ships pass down the Wantsum with the archbishop aboard. A man of Thorkell's is asking along the strand for wine, and he has silver that was Kent's last week.

The army lies at Greenwich and wants its price for the archbishop, who forbids anyone to pay it. The Saturday after Easter there is wine in the camp, brought from the south. Thorkell offers all he has but his ship to stop what follows.

In June King Cnut has the saint brought home from London and laid north of Christ's altar. The monks remember who paid in 1009, who carried in 1011, and whose wine it was. It is all written somewhere.

endings.how: Paid the house's share in 1009 and took the people and the church's chest down the river in 1011.
endings.text: The books winter in a store on Thanet and come home. When the saint is laid by the altar the house's name is read among those who stood by Kent, and the king, who likes such lists, hears it.
endings.reward: The flag en_paid_share; standing in Kent raised for a generation; the unlock fordwic.unlock.saints_neighbour; a word in King Cnut's ear toward en_cnut_peace; act:copy_text and act:lodge free at Christ Church.

endings.how: Sold the wine to the army at Greenwich.
endings.text: It is the best market of the year and you are paid in Kentish pennies. The Chronicle says only that the wine came from the south. At Canterbury they say whose keel it came in.
endings.reward: The flag en_followed_silver; silver, the best single cargo of the age; Thorkell's men friendly wherever they are met; at Fordwic the monks' doors shut and the toll taken to the last farthing until an heir makes it good with a gift at the saint's tomb.

endings.how: Lay elsewhere in 1009 and 1011 and came back when it was quiet.
endings.text: The house lost nothing and gave nothing. The reeve who reads out the toll is a new man, the old one having been taken with the rest. He does not know your face.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but what was known: every feeling at Fordwic begins again from easy, as for a stranger.

stories.reward: A name read out at a saint's tomb and a king's goodwill, or the richest cargo of the age and a shut door: decided by what a keel on the Stour did in three autumns.

works.name: A hythe of oak and wattle
works.what: A length of the river bank faced with oak posts and wattle and packed behind with gravel and flint, with a ramp for carts, so that a boat lies afloat alongside at half tide and unloads over a plank.
works.needs: The reeve at least friendly, and a plot of your own or leave from whoever owns the bank: the king until King Edward's gift, then the abbot.
works.gives: No waiting for the top of the tide to load at Fordwic; porters at half; act:careen and act:repair a day quicker. The reeve hangs your tally by the door, where it is seen.
works.picture: A straight timber-faced bank on a brown river with a small boat lying alongside it afloat, a plank ashore, a cart backed down a gravel ramp, reeds on the far side.
works.source: ours, in the manner of the timber and wattle waterfronts of the English wics; ships 'were moored' at the quay 'where all goods were laded and unladed' (Hasted, of the later port; dossier 1). Nothing of the kind has been dug at Fordwich (?)

works.name: A fenced plot of your own
works.what: A haga: a narrow plot from the track to the river inside a fence of wattle and thorn, with a house, a store raised on posts and a ditch to the water. Bought before witnesses and the reeve.
works.needs: Standing in Kent, two or three true men to witness, and a plot to be had: after a bad year there are several.
works.gives: act:store and act:lodge free at Fordwic; goods left here are safe between voyages; a factor can be set in it; from 1042 the house counts among the ninety-six plots and its keel is no longer a foreign merchant's to the reeve.
works.picture: A long narrow plot between wattle fences running down to a river: a thatched house by the track, a small store on posts, bales under a lean-to, a gate standing open.
works.source: the reeve's two hagas and a meadow at Fordwic (Sawyer 1654); ninety-six plots in 1066 (Domesday; dossier 2). Buying before witnesses or the reeve: Hlothhere and Eadric 16

works.name: A gospel book for Christ's altar
works.what: A book of the four gospels written at Christ Church at the house's cost: the skins of a herd of calves, a year of a scribe's life, and a cover with as much silver on it as you care to pay for.
works.needs: A scribe of Christ Church friendly, calfskin found (the story fordwic.calves_and_gold), and no war in Kent that year.
works.gives: The house's name written in the book to be prayed for; the archbishop of the day at least friendly to this merchant and the next heir; every monk on the book road has heard of it (bk_carried honoured without carrying). If the city is stormed the book may be carried off, and that is another story.
works.picture: A book lying open on an altar cloth under a lamp, its page ruled and half written in a round clear hand with one great coloured letter, a monk's inky hand resting beside it.
works.source: ours. Laymen gave books to Christ Church with their names written in to be prayed for: Ealdorman Alfred and Wærburh, in the Stockholm Codex Aureus (dossier 7). The cost is the game's (six pounds of pennies) (?)

works.name: A church at the landing
works.what: A small church of timber, then of flint with stone corners, on the rise behind the plots, so that Fordwic need not walk two miles to hear Mass. The stone comes by sea from the island of Wight.
works.needs: A plot of your own at Fordwic, the abbot of Saint Augustine's leave (the borough is his from King Edward's gift), and a priest found.
works.gives: A new site at Fordwic, a church of Saint Mary, with hear_mass, alms, vow and bury at the landing; the abbot a fast friend; the house's dead may lie here; the borough remembers who built it.
works.picture: A small plain church of flint with pale squared stones at its corners and a thatched roof, half built, scaffold poles lashed round it, the river and boats' masts just behind.
works.source: Saint Mary's at Fordwich was probably first built in the late eleventh century, its corner stones of Quarr stone from Wight (Tatton-Brown 1992); the county record calls the work 'Saxon' (Kent HER). No church can be shown here before then, and its dedication then is not known (dossier 2, 6, 8): that a merchant paid for it, and before 1066, is ours (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand, or built to order in six weeks
ships.note: The boat of the river and the marsh: six metres, four oars, for nets, eel traps and carrying hay. Somebody at the plots always has one upturned on trestles, half mended and for sale.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat upside down on trestles beside a wattle fence, a man tarring her seams, hens underneath.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat; unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_west_small_boat names Fordwic

ships.how: lent by the minster to a trusted master, not owned
ships.note: The ship of the charter: a Thanet minster's coaster, free of toll here by the old king's word, whose gains must be shown to the king's man at this hythe. She is lent to a merchant the house trusts, and Tilred will want to see what she earned.
ships.picture: A broad double-ended coaster of ten or eleven metres lying at a river bank, a small cross painted on her stem, a reeve with a white wand looking down into her from the gravel.
ships.source: Sawyer 29 (763 or 764); ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship; story/ships_793.json (lent, not built, at Fordwic, until about 870); unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_coaster_minster_ship and unlock_charter_fordwic

ships.note: Small trading boats of the house's own size come up on every spring tide for the churches' custom, and now and then one is sold at the hythe by a skipper who has had enough of the Wantsum's mud.
ships.picture: A small open trading boat with her mast lowered, afloat at a gravel bank among reeds, a man with his hands on his hips looking her over.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json gislinge; that one is for sale here is ours

ships.how: hired by the day, with a boy to pole her
ships.note: A flat marsh boat for the ditches and the last shallow reach. She will lighten a laden keel that cannot get up to the hythe on a small tide, a few bales at a time.
ships.picture: A narrow flat-bottomed boat in a reed-edged ditch, a boy standing in her stern with a pole, three bales amidships.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json skiff_punt; the river is tidal to Fordwich and shallow above (dossier 1). That one can be hired here is ours

sayings.text: Two miles to the city by the track. Three, if the man is carrying your goods.
sayings.source: invented, on the two measures of the Fordwich track: two miles in Hasted (1800), three in Tatton-Brown (1992) (dossier 1)

sayings.text: Fordwic takes the toll and the city takes the thanks.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the toll is taken at the landing (Sawyer 29), the churches and the market are in Canterbury

sayings.text: Then was a captive he who before was of England head and Christendom.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1011, of Archbishop Ælfheah (Ingram 1823, with Giles's additions)

sayings.text: They were also much drunken; for there was wine brought them from the south.
A friend is good far or near; the nearer, the more use.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, about 1050, older in the mouth; the rendering of Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.md from the Old English 'Freond deah feor ge neah: byth near nyttra'

sayings.text: Three fingers hold the pen, and the whole back pays for it.
sayings.source: the common scribes' colophon ('three fingers write, the whole body labours'), in our words; said here by Eadhun

sayings.text: A book is a herd of calves that has learned Latin.
sayings.source: invented, a writing-room joke: on Tatwine's riddle of parchment (texts_793.json tatwine_05_membranis) and the spine's reckoning of a book's cost (thread book_road)

sayings.text: The archbishop made forty riddles and died. Eusebius made sixty and nobody knows who he was. Brevity, says the scribe, has its reward.
sayings.source: invented, a monk's dry joke on a true thing: Tatwine's forty and Eusebius's sixty (dossier 7)

sayings.text: The king asked the moneyer whose face he liked best on a penny. The moneyer said: the one that is paying me.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, a proverb turned; on the Canterbury moneyers of 796-798 and of about 822-824, who were unsure whose name to use (dossier 4)

sayings.text: Blow your horn on the marsh, or be a thief till somebody has time to ask.
sayings.source: the sense of the Law of Wihtred (695), not its words: a stranger off the track who neither shouts nor blows his horn (dossier 6)

sayings.text: Even the rats in Canterbury eat charters.
sayings.source: invented, on a true thing: the charter that names the cnihts' guild has a hole cut by rats (Sawyer 1199, notes; dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: A small thick silver piece turns up in Cwengyth's egg money with a man's name on it in runes: Æthiliræd. Nobody alive can say who he was. Eoba will give its weight for it and no more.
easter_eggs.source: a sceat of Series E with the name Æthiliræd in runes (700-710), found at Fordwich (Kent HER, MKE76906; dossier 2)

easter_eggs.text: A penny of Offa lost in the gravel on the Sturry side has its moneyer's name, Wihtræd, written partly in runes: a man from the East Angles' mint who could not decide which letters a king preferred.
easter_eggs.source: a penny of Offa, East Anglian mint, 770-792, the moneyer Wihtræd's name partly in runes, found at Sturry (Kent HER, MKE76993; dossier 2)

easter_eggs.text: The leaf that gives away land at Sturry, just over the ford, is shown in the abbey's chest: a king's gift of the year 679, in the hand that first wrote it. It will be the oldest English charter of its kind to survive.
easter_eggs.source: Sawyer 8 (679), the oldest English charter surviving as first written (dossier 2). That it lay at the abbey is ours (?)

easter_eggs.text: From 858 a leaf in the city's chest names 'the cnihts' guild' among its witnesses. Ask to see it in a later age and there is a neat hole in it. Rats.
easter_eggs.source: Sawyer 1199 (858 x 866) and its notes: a hole cut by rats (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: King Wihtred's law is dated the sixth day of Rugern. Wicga still calls the rye harvest by that name, and no other month by any name at all.
easter_eggs.source: the Law of Wihtred (695), dated in 'Rugern', the rye harvest (dossier 6)

easter_eggs.text: Stodmarsh means the mares' marsh. The mares have been on it since before the place had a charter, and the charter is of 675.
easter_eggs.source: Sawyer 7 (675), 'Stodmerch'; the name's meaning from the dossier (3)

easter_eggs.text: The ale-house trout is as long as a forearm. Eight hundred and sixty years after the game begins a fisherman will write that the trout of this one river are the best in England.
easter_eggs.source: the Stour's big trout, famous by 1653 (dossier 4)

easter_eggs.text: After 1031, ask at the abbey how far Christ Church's rights at Sandwich reach, and a monk of the other house will show you with his arm: as far as a tall man can throw a small axe from a ship afloat at the highest tide.
In 1012 a man of the army says quietly that Thorkell offered everything he owned for the archbishop's life, except his ship.
easter_eggs.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, through the dossier (7; Siege of Canterbury)

easter_eggs.text: A grey-haired clerk keeps the feast of Saint Æthelheard on the twelfth day of May. No one will keep it after the Normans come.
easter_eggs.source: Æthelheard, kept as a saint on 12 May until Lanfranc ended it (dossier 6)

unlocks.how: Buy Tatwine's leaf of the sword and its sheath from the scribe (14 d; Latin, or a reader aboard) and answer it yourself before the reeve: the ending 'answered' of fordwic.sword_and_sheath.
unlocks.gives: rw_toll_fordwic (riddles_793.json): toll none on your ship at Fordwic for some years.

unlocks.what: The abbess's freedom, shown at Fordwic
unlocks.how: Hold the Thanet minster's freedom (sarre.abbess_freedom) or master one of its ships, and offer her season's gains to the king's man at this hythe unasked, as the charter says.
unlocks.gives: unlock_charter_fordwic: toll none on this ship here. It lapses if captives or arms are carried under it, if standing with the minster falls, and when the king who confirmed it dies, until an audience and a gift renew it.

unlocks.what: Archbishop Tatwine's riddles, by the leaf
unlocks.how: Bought from the scribe at Christ Church: parchment (12 d), snow, hail and ice (12 d), the sword and its sheath (14 d). Latin is needed, or a reader aboard.
unlocks.gives: give_text tatwine_05_membranis, tatwine_15_nive_glacie, tatwine_30_ense_vagina (unlocks_793.json text.tatwine_05_membranis and the others). From 928 a canon sells three of Aldhelm's as well, at 16 d.

unlocks.what: The ten chickens and the thing with many teeth
unlocks.how: Buy twice from Cwengyth and guess what walked out of the yard; be trusted by Wicga and name what he is holding.
unlocks.gives: give_text exeter_13_ten_chickens and exeter_34_rake (unlocks_793.json text.exeter_13_ten_chickens, text.exeter_34_rake); the chickens pay the riddle's own reward, rw_silver_big.

unlocks.what: Your word taken at the moneyers' benches
unlocks.how: End 'Whose name on the penny' on Eoba's word; or bring him strange silver first on five calls.
unlocks.gives: change_coin at Canterbury at half the loss, and test_silver free, for this merchant and half as well for the first heir.

unlocks.what: A seat at Christ Church and a letter to anyone you name
unlocks.how: Carry the church's book chest over the water in 796-798 (dofras.archbishops_chest, the ending over_the_water), or end 'What is in a man's bundle' with two letters.
unlocks.gives: An audience with the archbishop never refused while Æthelheard lives; one letter of introduction to a bishop, abbot or reeve of your choosing in England or Francia: the feeling of that person begins at friendly.

unlocks.what: What a book is worth, and to whom
unlocks.how: Bring Eadhun thirty calfskins before winter (the first half of fordwic.calves_and_gold).
unlocks.gives: The flags bk_knows_worth and bk_parchment: you can price a book in a heathen market, and Christ Church gives a standing commission for calfskin, pigments and wax each year.

unlocks.what: A name read at Saint Ælfheah's tomb
unlocks.how: End 'He who was England's head' having paid in 1009 and carried in 1011.
unlocks.gives: lodge and copy_text free at Christ Church for the house and its heirs; toll at half at Fordwic while there are monks in Canterbury; pilgrims to the tomb ask for passage in your keel by name (a commission that comes again each spring from 1023).

unlocks.what: What the port-reeve took unjustly, given back
unlocks.how: From 1042, be a fast friend of Bruman, or own a plot at Fordwic and bring a suit before the shire with two witnesses.
unlocks.gives: The customs taken from the house at Fordwic since 1042 returned in silver, once; after it, no more than the lawful toll while Bruman is reeve.
